In 3D the ray from the camera's pose at that frame through the pointer meets the plane, or the terrain plate's height samples as the two triangles per sample quad that its height-field collision uses, at its nearest hit, rounded to 1/1024 m; a ray that meets nothing gives none. A box's four corners are the rays through the screen rectangle's corners, in order from the press corner clockwise on screen, each met the same way. `hit` names the topmost drawn row, element or item of `targets` under the pointer at the press, by the core's hit test, skipping any that doesn't draw (Control: picks on rows and grid focus). Every 3D entry also stores the ray through the pointer, its origin at the camera's eye, or on the near plane for an orthographic camera, and its unit direction, so an input derived from the entry or a logic step can throw along it however the camera turns afterwards. With `on: surface`, the object-ID target names the topmost drawn target under the pointer, as a pick does, and `hit` records it, while the ray meets that item's mesh as the CPU evaluates it at the gesture's flick (a skinned or morphed item's vertices as checks read them, an instancer's element under its evaluated transform), in the same pinned f64 math, and its nearest triangle gives `face`, its index among the item's triangles in draw order, `point`, rounded to 1/1024 m, `normal`, the triangle's unit normal in world space by its winding, and `uv`, the item's uv0 at the point by its barycentric weights, or none where the mesh has no uv0. A ray that misses that item's triangles, as at its silhouette, gives surface none. An expression reads a point control's value by field, such as `<control>.ray.dir` or `<control>.surface.normal`, each a vec3. A drag that starts with one of the control's buttons over its view belongs to the control, so the camera's plain-drag pan moves to keys, the middle button or the edge (Camera `camera@1`: goto and edge pan). `hover` is the cell or ground point under the pointer, computed the same way as it moves: a viewer-class value that drivers may read to place a ghost, that a logic item's steps may not read (refused at check, naming the read), though its preview may (Logic: preview), and that goldens, exports and checks evaluate as none. On a grid set the control takes the rows' keyboard focus, and Enter writes a press and a release at the focused cell.

**Cost:** A 2D cell O(1); a ray against a plane O(1), against a terrain plate O(sample cells it crosses), under 0.1 ms on a 4,097² plate (estimate); a ray against a surface O(log triangles) through a hierarchy built once per mesh content key, or O(triangles) for an item whose vertices move, such as a skinned one, about 1 ms for 100,000 (estimate); an entry 248 B on the track. Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Compute a point again on replay; put hover on the input track or in a logic step; hit a row or element that doesn't draw; compute a ground point or a surface hit on the GPU

**Lands:** R6, with the logic module

#### Control: actions, key repeat and gamepads

For: games with many commands: walk, wait, open, fire, an inventory, menus that change what keys mean, play from a gamepad, and looking around with the mouse in first person

**Fields**

- `kind: actions` (beside the others; class document)
- `actions: {name → {keys: [key chord], pad: [button], key_repeat: {delay: s = 0.4, rate: Hz = 10} | none = none}} ≤ 256`
- `contexts: {name → [action name]} ≤ 32` (numbered from 0 in declaration order)
- `context: <logic>.<name> | none = none` (an i32 array of count 1 that picks the context, read through the core's column view: Array and table: column view; with none, context 0)
- `sticks: {left | right → {dead_zone: 0..1 = 0.2}}` (optional)
- `look: {buttons: [primary | secondary] = [primary]} | none = none` (the mouse's motion while the pointer is locked: Input router, focus and gesture serial)
- Pad buttons: `south | east | west | north | l1 | r1 | l2 | r2 | select | start | l3 | r3 | up | down | left | right`
- Values: an action's index in `actions` with `repeat: u16` (0 for the press); a stick's `{stick, x, y}`, each from −64 to 64 (coarse; fine sticks: Control: actions: held actions and fine sticks); a look's `{dx, dy}` (i32), the pointer's motion over one step in 1/16 px
- In a logic item's read region, 16 B: `u32 tag` (0 an action, 1 a stick, 2 a look), `u32` the action's index, the stick (0 left, 1 right) or 0 (a look's: 1 when `raw`, Control: actions: held actions and fine sticks), `i32` the repeat, x or dx, `i32` 0, y or dy
- Issue: `actions.context {value, step}`

**Semantics:** A press of a key chord or a pad button that an action in the current context holds writes one entry with that action's index, at the gesture. The current context is the one the `context` array names as the logic module gives it at the gesture's flick, resolved once there and recorded as the action, so a replay reads the action and never resolves it again; a value naming no context resolves nothing and raises `actions.context`, naming the value and the step. A press no action in the context holds writes nothing, and two actions in one context holding the same chord or button are refused at check, naming both. With `key_repeat`, a key or button held past `delay` writes one more entry, with repeat k, for each time the press's flick + delay + (k − 1) ÷ rate that comes before its release, each stamped at the first logic step at or after that time; the times come from the press's flick alone, never from frames or the wall clock, so a hold of one length writes the same entries at any frame rate, and each is an ordinary recorded entry. Pad buttons and sticks arrive through the input seam (Seam and backend), whose backends read the platform's game controllers, and on the web the page's gamepads, as input from you with gesture serials, like keys, so an agent or a synthetic event can't send one. A coarse stick maps each axis outside `dead_zone` to round(64 × its value) and inside it to 0, and writes an entry when that pair changes, at most one a step. With `look`, a press of one of its buttons in the piece's view, with your gesture serial, locks the pointer (Input router, focus and gesture serial), writes no entry and reaches no other control. While it's locked, each motion the input seam reads is rounded to 1/16 px once, as it arrives, and the motions stamped on one step sum into one look entry, written when the sum isn't zero, so a replay reads the entries and never the pointer, and the same motions give the same entries at any frame rate. The pointer stays hidden at the view's center, so a point control's press while locked aims along the camera's axis. A piece's logic turns dx and dy into its own turn. A look is refused at check in a document of class figure, data view or core view, and a document shown inside another, such as on a return card, never locks.

**Cost:** A lookup O(1) a press; a repeat O(1); an entry about 32 B on the track. Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Stamp a repeat by frames or the wall clock; resolve an action again on replay; take a pad input from an agent; let two actions in one context hold one key; lock the pointer without your press in its view, or keep it locked past Esc, the piece losing focus, the question card or an ask; lock in a figure or in a document shown inside another

**Lands:** R6, with the logic module; pads with the input seam's backends

#### Control: actions: held actions and fine sticks

For: real-time games: walking while a key is down, firing while a button is held, charging while a trigger is pulled, a round that pauses when Esc ends the pointer lock, and fine aim with a stick

**Fields**

- On an action: `release: bool = false` (with true, letting go writes a release entry)
- On `look`: `lock_end: bool = false` (with true, the Esc that ends the lock writes one entry)
- Values: a release, the index of the action its press recorded; a lock end, its cause (`esc`)
- In a logic item's read region, 16 B as before: tag 3 a release (`u32 3`, `u32` the action's index, `i32 0`, `i32 0`); tag 4 a lock end (`u32 4`, `u32` its cause, 0 for Esc, `i32 0`, `i32 0`)
- `sticks` also take `shape: axis | radial = axis` and `precision: coarse | fine = coarse` (fine: each axis an i16 from −32,767 to 32,767; coarse keeps −64 to 64)
- A look's value gains `raw: bool` (true when the motion came before the platform's pointer acceleration)
- In a logic item's read region: a look's second `u32` is 1 when `raw`, else 0; a fine stick's x and y fill its two `i32` fields

**Semantics:** With `release`, letting go of the last key of the chord, or the button, that pressed an action writes one release entry, stamped as a press is, with the action the press recorded, never resolved again in the context current at the release, so a context that changes while a key is down still releases what the press started. A release is your gesture, the key or the button let go, with its own serial. A key or a button let go while the piece lacks keyboard focus reaches no piece, so its release is written at your next input in the piece, as part of that input's gesture and carrying its serial, before the input itself; until then the piece reads the action as held. With `lock_end`, the Esc that ends a look's lock (Input router, focus and gesture serial) writes one lock-end entry carrying Esc's serial, and nothing else for Esc; a lock that ends any other way writes nothing. A held key's repeats stop at its release. Logic reads a held action as the fold of its presses and releases, a level: no entry means nothing changed, which is what a match predicts for a player whose message hasn't come (Net: rollback), so a hold costs one entry at each end, never one a step. With `precision: fine`, each axis outside the dead zone maps to round(32,767 × its value); with `shape: radial`, the pair maps to (0, 0) while its length is inside `dead_zone` and otherwise keeps both axes, so a diagonal never snaps to an axis; either way an entry comes at most once a step, when the pair changes, and the piece's logic applies its own response curve. The input seam's backends read a look's motion before the platform's pointer acceleration where the platform offers it, on macOS through the Game Controller framework's mouse and on the web through Pointer Lock's `unadjustedMovement`, and otherwise its accelerated motion, marking each look entry `raw` or not; the 1/16 px rounding and the step's sum stay as they are.

**Cost:** A release or a lock end O(1) and about 32 B on the track, once per hold, where a repeat standing in for a held key would cost one a step; fine sticks as coarse ones. Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Release an action its press didn't record, or resolve a release's action again; write a release or a lock end without a gesture of yours and its serial; snap a radial stick's axis to 0 on a diagonal; mark accelerated motion `raw`

**Lands:** R6, with the logic module; pads and unaccelerated motion with the input seam's backends

#### Control: text

For: words and code a player types into a piece's rules: a unit's name, a processor's program, a line of chat in a match

**Fields**

- `text: {max_bytes: u32 ≤ 16,384 = 256, lines: one | many = one}` (on a control of kind text; class document)
- Value: the field's UTF-8 bytes
- In a logic item's read region: `u32` length, the bytes, then zero bytes to the next multiple of 8 from the length's start

**Semantics:** A text control carries what you type to a piece's logic as bytes. It writes one entry when you commit: Enter with `lines: one`; with `lines: many`, Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter off macOS) or leaving the field, where Enter adds a line. The entry holds the field's whole content as UTF-8 bytes exactly as typed, never normalized, with line ends as LF: a pasted CR LF or CR becomes LF, and with `lines: one` a pasted line end is refused. Typing stops at `max_bytes`, and a paste that would pass it is refused whole with a notice naming the cap, never cut. Keys and input-method text reach it only through the input router with your serial, and an agent writes it only through the parameter tool, stamped as that writer. At most one commit of a control is stamped a step, and a second waits for the next step, so a logic item that reads it reserves 4 + max_bytes, rounded up to a multiple of 8, in its read region. Its bytes are on the input track, so saves, replays, rollback and peers carry them like any entry.

**Cost:** An entry is its bytes plus about 32 B on the track, at most about 16 KiB; filling the read region O(bytes). Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Normalize, cut or re-encode the bytes; take more than `max_bytes`; be typed by an agent except through the parameter tool; run what it carries anywhere but in the piece's logic

**Lands:** R6, with the logic module

#### Control: kinds as a registry

For: adding a control kind only with proof that it replays, reaches the keyboard and takes no agent input, while packs build widgets from the kinds that exist

**Fields**

- `control@1` registry (Registry and seal: registries): `{owner: input, fill: [module], resolve: seal}`
- Entry: `{name, classes: [document | view | viewer], sources: [pointer | keys | wheel | pad | a device class], value: {fields}, read_region: {bytes, layout digest}, role: ARIA role, keyboard: path | fallback (device)}`
- Kit: `{replay, read_region, keyboard, input}`, with a planted wrong entry for each part

**Semantics:** The input module (`input@1`), split from motion, holds controls and the input track's handling, picks, the point control, actions, key repeat, pads, text, scroll, device controls, bridges' entries and ports; motion keeps clips, channels, drivers, constraints, shots, transitions, cues and eases. The input module declares `control@1`, and every control kind is an entry: slider, toggle, choice, stages, transport, drag_along, turn, press, text, hover, point, actions, scroll and device. Only canvas modules fill it, at the seal, since every entry rides the input router, which is ring; a pack or a plug-in builds widgets from these kinds (Pack: programs) and never adds one. Each entry passes the kit at the seal. Replay: its entries are computed once, at the gesture, and stored, so a replay, a seek and every peer read them and never compute them again, and a fixture recorded at 30, 60 and 120 frames a second gives one track hash. Read region: its layout's digest matches what logic reads. Keyboard: it has a role and a keyboard path, so it works without a pointer; a device control's path is its `fallback`, and the kit checks that each one names a control a keyboard can operate. Input: it takes no entry without your gesture serial, except an agent's through the parameter tool, stamped as that writer, and a device control's from a bridge, which the kit checks are stamped `plugin` with no gesture serial while its hardware entries carry their serial (Control: device bridges). A kind that fails a part is refused at the seal, naming the kind and the part, and each of the kit's planted wrong entries, such as a kind whose value is computed again from the camera on replay, or a device kind that gives a bridge's entries a serial, must fail.

**Cost:** The kit at the seal and in the local preflight, a few seconds of recorded fixtures (estimate); nothing per frame

**It can never:** Take a kind from a pack or a plug-in; skip a kit part; compute an entry again on replay; take input from an agent except through the parameter tool

**Lands:** R6, with the input module, before the kinds that game input and device controls add

#### Control: scroll

For: a list longer than its frame, such as an inventory, a log, a shop or a scoreboard, scrolled by the wheel, a trackpad or keys

**Fields**

- `kind: scroll` (class view by default, or document)
- `scroll: {axis: x | y = y, step: u = 24, range: [i32, i32], page: steps = 10, area: item ID}`
- Value: an `i32` position in steps; in a logic item's read region, 8 B: `i32 position, i32 delta`

**Semantics:** While the pointer is over its area, wheel and trackpad deltas scroll it instead of zooming the camera; elsewhere the camera keeps the wheel. Deltas become whole steps once, at the gesture: a wheel line is one step, and pixel deltas count one step for each `step` they cover on screen, the rest carried until the gesture ends and then dropped. Each change writes one entry with the new position, clamped to its range, so a replay reads the entries and never quantizes again. With focus, the arrows move a step, Page Up and Page Down a page, and Home and End go to the ends, and the position is announced by its `value_text`. In class view it's session state, never on the input track, and goldens, exports and checks read its default; in class document it's on the track like any entry. A mark set, a group's offset or a logic item reads the position, so a list draws the rows from there to its visible count; with smoothing, the drawn offset follows in closed form.

**Cost:** O(1) per delta; an entry about 24 B on the track (estimate)

**It can never:** Quantize again on replay; take the wheel outside its area; scroll by frames or the wall clock; pass its range

**Lands:** R6, with the logic module

#### Control: device

For: a piece played with a device keys and the pointer don't cover: a pen's pressure in a drawing toy, two-finger turns on a tablet, a pad's tilt, notes from a MIDI keyboard

**Fields**

- `kind: device` (beside the others: an entry of the input module's control kinds registry)
- `device: {class: name@major, filter: {field → [min, max]} (optional, such as a note range), from: input | plug-in ID = input}`
- `class: document | viewer` (document puts its entries on the input track; by default the device class's own)
- `fallback: control ID` (required: a control in the document a keyboard can operate, which the piece reads for the same job, such as a slider for a pen's pressure or actions for notes)
- Value: one entry in the class's layout
- In a logic item's read region: a `u32` count and 4 zero bytes, then each entry as a `u32` player, 4 zero bytes and the class's bytes padded to a multiple of 8, at most the class's `max_per_step` a step

**Semantics:** A device control reads one device class (Seam and backend: device classes). With class document, each input the class's backend delivers that passes the filter writes one entry at the gesture, stamped from the event's own time by the input track's rule, as a key's entry is; past `max_per_step` the rest wait for the next step, in order. A replay, a seek and every peer read the entry and never read the device again. With class viewer, its latest value is session state that drivers may read, as hover is, and a logic step may not (refused at check, naming the read). With `from` naming a plug-in, the control reads the entries that plug-in's bridge sends for the class instead (Control: device bridges). Like any control it has a role and a label that names the device; its keyboard path is its `fallback`, and one whose fallback is missing or names a control no keyboard can operate is refused at check, naming both; and an agent writes its entries only through the parameter tool, stamped as itself.

**Cost:** A lookup O(1) per input; an entry its class's bytes plus about 16 B on the track. Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Read the device again on replay; put a viewer-class value on the input track or in a logic step; take an agent's entry except through the parameter tool; count a bridge's entry as yours; play without a fallback a keyboard can operate

**Lands:** R6, with the input seam's device classes

#### Control: device bridges

For: gear the input seam doesn't read: a phone used as a tilt controller, an eye tracker, a lighting desk's faders, a sensor on a lab bench

**Fields**

- Plug-in side: `deep.registerDevice(class, bridge)` (the tech design's Extension API); `class`: a registered device class, or the plug-in's own `ext.<plug-in>.<name>@major` with a fixed layout of at most 256 B, an entry of `device.class@1` with no backend that passes the class kit at install (Seam and backend: device classes)
- Access word in the manifest: `device:<class>`, approved once
- Entry, as the core stamps it: `{t: flick, seq, writer: plugin, plugin: ID, class, value}`
- Waiting: at most the class's `max_per_step` a step, up to 64 waiting; past that, dropped and counted
- Issue: `device.dropped {plugin, class, count}`

**Semantics:** A bridge is a hub plug-in that reads gear itself, in its own process under its grant, and streams entries for one class into the canvas. The core stamps each entry on arrival, at the first step not yet run (in a match, `delay` match steps later, as a key's entry is), with the writer `plugin` and the plug-in's ID taken from its connection, never from the entry, and checks its bytes against the class's layout, refusing one that doesn't fit and naming the class. It delivers entries only to device controls whose `from` names that plug-in, on the piece you focused or the one present mode shows; entries for any other piece are dropped and counted. A bridge never mints a gesture serial, so its entries can't move focus, start sound, open a port, answer an ask or reach a panel. They're recorded like any entry, so a replay, a seek and a peer read them without the plug-in, and a requirement about what you did never counts them as yours. A class a plug-in declares is listed with the registries, named as that plug-in's, and binds only claims that name it.

**Cost:** One stream per bridge, outside the hub's event loop once approved; each entry checked on arrival in O(bytes) (estimate). Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Mint or carry a gesture serial; stamp its own time or step; write as you or as another plug-in; reach a piece you haven't focused, or a panel; send to a control that doesn't name it

**Lands:** R6, with the extension host's streams

#### Control: touch zones

For: playing a real-time game on a phone: a movement stick under the left thumb, look by dragging on the right, and buttons in the right thumb's arc

**Fields**

- `kind: touch_zones` (beside the others; class document; reads `touches@1`)
- `zones: {name → {anchor: corner | edge, offset: [px, px], shape: {circle: {radius: px}} | {rect: {w, h: px}}, role: {action: name} | {stick: left | right, travel: px} | {look: {gain: f32 = 1}}}} ≤ 16` (a design cap: two thumbs need a few zones, and each contact that goes down tests every one)
- `actions: control ID` (the actions control whose actions and sticks the zones write; it's the zones' keyboard fallback)
- `edge_clear: px = 32` (estimate: about what phones keep at their edges for system gestures)
- Anchors: `<control>#<zone>`, each zone's center and shape, which overlays and marks read
- On `verb: canvas.full_screen`: `orientation: any | landscape | portrait = any`

**Semantics:** A touch-zones control turns a phone's contacts into the entries the actions control already writes, so one piece's logic plays with keys, a pad or thumbs alike. The core lays the zones out in the view's own pixels, anchored as overlays are, inside the safe area; a zone closer than `edge_clear` to an edge, or two zones that overlap, at any size the layout check runs, is refused at check, naming them. One listener per view takes every contact: a contact belongs to the zone it went down in until it lifts or cancels, wherever it slides, and one that went down in no zone writes nothing. An action zone writes its action's press when its first contact goes down and its release when its last one lifts (Control: actions: held actions and fine sticks); a stick zone writes stick entries from its contact's offset from where it went down, divided by `travel` and held to the unit disc, with the stick's own dead zone, shape and precision; a look zone writes look entries from its contact's motion in 1/16 px times `gain`. A contact that cancels, as an edge gesture's does, ends its zone's gesture as a lift would. Each entry is computed once at the gesture from the recorded contacts and stamped as a touches entry is, so a replay and every peer read the entries, never the contacts again. A zone draws nothing itself: each is an anchor, so the button an overlay or a mark draws sits exactly on it. With `orientation: landscape`, entering full screen asks the browser or the platform to hold landscape where it offers that, and where it doesn't, the piece shows its own hint.

**Cost:** A hit test O(zones) per contact that goes down; entries as the actions control's. Budget class: as the control.

**It can never:** Write an entry the actions control couldn't write from a key, a pad or the mouse; hand a contact to another zone; place a zone within `edge_clear` of an edge or outside the safe area; take a contact from an agent or a synthetic event

**Lands:** R6, with the input seam's device classes

#### Input track

**Fields**

- `entries: [{t: flick, seq: u32, control | physics input | reading, value, samples: polyline (optional), writer: you | tour | agent | bot | peer | net}]`
- `writer` also takes `plugin`: a device bridge's entries, with the plug-in's ID (Control: device bridges)
- `fork_at: flick`
- `checkpoint_every: s = 0.5`
- Present mode's keys write entries too: `{t, seq, present: advance | back, writer}` (Marker: present mode)

**Semantics:** A frame reads only entries at or before its flick, and physics inputs are entries too, those a logic item fires among them, as derived entries that follow from its steps and are never stored (Input track entries). `draw.commit` and `draw.reveal` are entry kinds the core holds, which the net module writes (Net: random draws after commit), and `net.draws`, the step's draw a logic item reads, is the core's, derived from the track's reveal entries by that section's rule, so a logic item reads it from the track and never names the net module. A seek or a scrub only moves the playhead: what it shows comes from the recorded entries up to its flick, restored from the nearest checkpoint and replayed, and every later entry stays, so the track's hash is unchanged and playing on plays the recorded future. A new entry where later entries exist, as after a seek back, forks the track at its flick: the later entries are dropped, `fork_at` records the flick, and the track's hash changes. An agent writes entries only through the parameter tool, stamped as itself. An entry's stamp comes from its input's `t`, the platform's timestamp of the event, or for a bridge the core's arrival time, never the plug-in's. That time is mapped onto the clock, through the audio clock's host-time pairing while sound plays. The stamp is the first step or sample at or after that position plus the input lead, or the first step not yet run or sample not yet written, whichever is later. The lead is one step while silent, and the write-ahead plus one block while sound plays, so what a gesture starts sounds and shows at the same flick live and on replay, and no stamp depends on the frame rate. A reading a logic item reads is an entry too, with its source and as-of time, stamped at the first step not yet run for each value its source delivers (Logic: readings), so a replay reads what the run read. Each entry also carries its player, 1 for a piece played alone and 1 to 8 in a match, where a peer's entries carry the writer `peer`. A peer's entry that arrives late is no fork: it joins the track at its step, never at its arrival, ordered there by step, player and seq, and drops nothing, so the track a match records is the one every entry would have made on time (Net). In a playtest, a replica's copy also takes a bot's entries, with the writer `bot`, at the steps they're stamped for, and records them like any other, so the run replays from its track alone; no other copy takes them (Check input: playtest).

**Cost:** O(log N) lookup; O(1) append; about 32 B per entry; a seek costs O(entries since the last checkpoint)

**It can never:** Be rewritten except by a fork; change on a seek or a scrub alone; carry wall-clock times; hold view or viewer inputs

**Lands:** R6

#### Port

For: a piece that drives gear or a service while you play: notes to a synthesizer, cues to stage lights, moves to your own game server, a pulse on a plug-in's controller

**Fields**

- `ports: {name → {plugin: plug-in ID, out: [control ID | occurrence list] (optional), in: [reading ID] (optional), sound: bool = false}} ≤ 8` (on the document)
- Connect prompt: `{port, plugin, hosts: [host] (its grant's), out, in, sound}` (the app's own, never the piece's)
- Out: `{port, step, t: flick, entries: [entry] | rows: [occurrence row]}`
- Plug-in side: `deep.registerPort(name, port)` (the tech design's Extension API): the entries and rows it takes, and the sources it provides for `in`
- `state: closed | open | stopped`

**Semantics:** A port is a piece's declared way out to one plug-in and back. Nothing flows until a person clicks Connect on a prompt the app draws, never the piece, naming the plug-in, the hosts its grant names and what goes out and comes in; it needs a gesture serial from hardware input, so a tour, a piece's logic, an agent's tool, a bridge or a replica can't open one. While it's open, each entry of a listed control and each row of a listed occurrence list goes to the plug-in once, in step order, as the piece plays live and forward; in a match, only once its step is confirmed, so a step a rollback replaced never goes out. A seek, a scrub, a replay, a render-back, a check and an export send nothing, and nothing a port sends feeds back into a frame, so seeking still equals playing. What comes in is readings from the plug-in's sources, which the piece reads like any reading and the input track records with their as-of times (Logic: readings), so a replay needs no plug-in; in a match, only the copy of the player the piece names in `readings_from` takes them in, and they travel as its entries. A port with `sound: true`, or whose plug-in's port says its gear makes sound, drives gear that makes sound, so its plug-in is a device gate owner whatever the document says: Connect needs a gesture in the piece's panel, and a mute or quiet hours stop the out side and tell the plug-in to fall silent. A port carries only what the document lists: never state, pixels, sound or anything about the viewer. It closes when the piece closes, when you close it or when its plug-in stops, and each Connect asks again. The web player's bundle carries no port: its export drops each one, naming it in the receipt's `refused`.

**Cost:** Out: about 32 B plus each entry's or row's bytes, once per step that has any; in: as readings; nothing per frame. Budget class: as the controls it lists.

**It can never:** Open without a person's Connect; send on a seek, a scrub, a replay, a check or an export; send a step a match hasn't confirmed; carry state, pixels, sound or anything about the viewer; reach a plug-in the document doesn't name

**Lands:** R6, with the extension host's streams

#### Tour

**Fields**

- `tour: {keys: {control → [[t, value, interp]]}, idle_after: s = 1.4, resume_after: s = 3.6, loop: bool = true}`

**Semantics:** Replays as input entries from the writer `tour` while you're idle. It yields at your first gesture and resumes after `resume_after` of quiet. Its entries derive from the track and your idle times, so a replay and a golden match.

**Cost:** That of its entries

**It can never:** Override your input; run under reduced motion; count as your gesture

**Lands:** R6

#### `start_on` and `switch`

**Fields**

- `start_on: {control, each: entry | change, policy: restart | overlap | ignore}`, or `start_on: {on: <logic ID>.occurrences + filter, policy}` (a logic item's occurrences: Logic: occurrences)
- `switch: {span: flick, ease | spring, sync: none | next_loop_phase}`

**Semantics:** `start_on` starts a placement run at each matching entry's flick, or at the time of each matching occurrence of a logic item, read from its bake through the core's column view (Array and table: column view), so a seek starts it where playing does and the motion module doesn't depend on logic. `switch` cross-fades when a choice changes: mix = ease((t − tc) ÷ span). If a case ever needs guards on a current mode, a mode machine would be a fold over the input track with checkpoints and at most 8 changes per flick.

**Cost:** O(log E) per frame; a seek costs O(entries since the last checkpoint)

**It can never:** Pick at random; integrate a mix with dt; exceed 8 changes per flick

**Lands:** R6

#### Transition

**Fields**

- `from, to: adjacent placements, shots or strips` (a `match_morph` may also name two items in one shot)
- `kind: cut | cross_fade | dip | wipe | push | iris | zoom_through | match_morph | text_diff | operator` (operator, iris and dip fields: the next row)
- `match_morph {pairs: {part → part}, unpaired: fade | morph | cross_fade | split = fade}`
- `span: flick`; `align: start | center | end | reveal = center`
- `overlap: bool` (false: an overlay at the cut)
- `progress` (from the look's time feel)
- `carry: [ID]` (items carried across)
- `wipe {angle: deg = 0, feather: px = 0}`; `push {angle: deg = 0}`; `zoom_through {center: ID[#anchor] | [f32, f32] = [0.5, 0.5]}` (angle 0 moves from the left edge to the right, 90 from the top down)

**Semantics:** Both sides evaluate at their own local times inside the window, draw offscreen, then blend. Status colors never blend: inside the window they draw once, after the blend, from the outgoing side until the reveal and from the incoming side from then on. `match_morph` pairs items by ID, or by shape hash. It also pairs a mark set's or a graph's rows by key and a vector's parts by id, then what's left by shape hash in reading order; paired paths morph with their points matched at check (Channel and key), paired transforms and paints mix as channels do, and anything unpaired fades. `pairs` pairs the parts it names before any other pairing, and `unpaired` says what the rest does: fade, morph, cross-fade, or split into faded copies, so one part can become several. `text_diff` moves kept tokens and fades inserted and deleted ones, so a film about a change can show the diff moving. Its tokens are words, or a code item's own tokens, aligned line by line (Text text@1: code). On a track, at most two strips overlap, and each overlap carries exactly one transition. `reveal` puts the frame where the incoming side first covers half the picture (for a push, 90% of its travel) on the cut's time, so the reveal lands on the beat.

**Cost:** About 2× the frame inside the window

**It can never:** Span more than either neighbor; hide a cut a check needs; contain a reading hold or a checked moment; use a plug-in shader; recolor status

**Lands:** R1 cut; R6 the rest

#### Transition: operator, iris and dip

For: transitions made of the medium: a page turn, an ink bloom, a dot wipe, a mosaic; an iris that closes on a character; a dip to paper

**Fields**

- `kind: operator {op: gpu.pass@1 ID (from a pack), reads: [outgoing, incoming, progress]}`
- `iris: {center: ID[#anchor] | [f32, f32], radius: channel, hold_at: f32}`
- `dip: {color: role = ink}`

**Semantics:** An operator transition is a composed pass over the outgoing and incoming color targets, each finished in its own look and display-referred, and the transition's progress, checked and budgeted like any operator; both sides still evaluate at their own local times, and align: reveal measures coverage from the operator's output. An iris centers on an evaluated item, so it follows a character. A dip takes a role, never a literal or a status color.

**Cost:** About 2× the frame inside the window, plus the operator's declared cost. Budget class: as the film.

**It can never:** Carry shader text; read an earlier frame; contain a reading hold or a checked moment; recolor status.

**Lands:** R6

#### Time remap

**Fields**

- `target: placement | recipe instance`
- `map: channel (parent flick → child flick)`, or a preset: `reverse | hold_at | ramp | scrub {control}`
- Preset `replay {on: occurrence list + filter | control, before: flick = 2 s, after: flick = 0.5 s, rate: rational = 1/4}` (rate ≤ 1), whose target may also be `document`
- `clamp: bool = true`

**Semantics:** Applied after the offset and rate, and floored to a flick. Physics children read their bake at child time. A remap whose child time can pass its parent's, such as reverse, scrub or a map that runs ahead, is refused at check when its target reads the input track, a control, a view input or a world that takes inputs, as a look-ahead is, since inputs after t don't exist yet. Audio is muted unless the rate is constant. A replay starts at each matching flick tc that comes while none runs: its target shows child time tc − before + (t − tc) × rate until child time reaches tc + after, then parent time again. Its child time never passes its parent's, so a replay is allowed beside a world that takes inputs. The world keeps stepping to parent time, so a replay's end shows the live state without a stall, and a document-class entry during a replay ends it. Drivers read `<remap ID>.active` and `.progress`, for a tag that says it's a replay.

**Cost:** One channel plus the child's cost; a replay changes no world step

**It can never:** Remap the input track; remap audio non-linearly; give a check a remapped time; start a replay inside a running one, or run one faster than its parent

**Lands:** R6

#### Matte

**Fields**

- `source: ID` (a hidden item that still evaluates)
- `mode: alpha | alpha_inverted | luma | luma_inverted`
- `luma: linear | encoded = linear` (encoded: Rec. 709 weights on sRGB-encoded values, as Lottie players take it)
- `resolution: full | half = full`
- `applies_to: ID | collection`

**Semantics:** A mask whose coverage comes from another item's evaluated pixels, frame by frame. Luma is taken in linear light, or on sRGB-encoded values with luma: encoded, so an imported Lottie matte keeps its coverage: a mid-gray matte covers 0.214 in linear light and 0.5 encoded. It applies before tone mapping and before status colors.

**Cost:** The source's draw plus one composite

**It can never:** Hide or recolor a status color; read outside the document; be a plug-in shader

**Lands:** R6

#### Text animator and counter

**Fields**

- Animator: `units: grapheme | word | line`; `range: {from, to, falloff, offset}`; `shape: square | ramp | smooth`; `mode: add | subtract | multiply | min | max | difference`; `clamp: bool`; `strength: channel`; `props: {opacity, x, y, rotate, scale, color (OKLab), tracking, axis (a variable-font axis)}` and more, with `selectors` (Text animator and counter: selectors and properties); `order: index | reverse | seeded`
- Counter: `text: counter {source: bound value | driver, format, tabular: true}`

**Semantics:** Text animators and counters are the text module's, since they write glyph instance transforms and formatted strings; channels drive their fields as they drive any item's. Shaping runs only when the content key changes, with units by UAX #29. Coverage is taken at each unit's center and mapped to glyph instance transforms. A counter reformats only when its string changes.

**Cost:** Shaping about 0.2 µs per char on change; 10 to 20 ns per glyph per frame

**It can never:** Shape per frame; split a grapheme; typeset LaTeX; show a number without a source

**Lands:** R1 counters (formatted bound values); R6 the animator

#### Text animator and counter: selectors and properties

For: kinetic type, decode and glitch titles, staggered word builds, letters that turn in 3D

**Fields**

- `props` gains `pivot: [u, u]`, `shear: deg`, `shear_axis: deg`, `blur: px`, `stroke: {role, width: px}`, `hue: deg`, `saturation` and `brightness` (as `adjust` defines them), `line_height: u`, `tracking_anchor: 0..1`, `glyph_shift: {set: digits | upper | lower | symbols | [string], by: i32}`, and on 3D marks `rotate: [deg, deg, deg]` and `z: m`
- The range gains `basis: fraction | index = fraction`, `units: … | grapheme_no_space`, `shape: … | ramp_down | triangle | round` (ramp stays the ramp up), `ease: {high, low: −1..1 = 0}`, and `strength` from −1 to 1
- `selectors: [range | noise | field] ≤ 4`, each with `mode`; `noise {min: −1..1 = −1, max: −1..1 = 1, frequency: Hz = 2, correlation: 0..1 = 0.5, phase, spatial_phase: deg = 0, lock: bool = false, seed}`; `field {expr, fallback}` over `i, n, u, t, value` from the closed function list

**Semantics:** The animator's own range, shape, order and mode become its first selector, and the rest combine top to bottom by each one's mode. A noise selector draws lattice noise of (unit index, t, seed), shared across units by correlation, so seeking equals playing. A field selector is a numeric expression. Shaping stays once per content key, and selection runs per unit per frame. glyph_shift swaps a grapheme for one in its set, shaped once at check, keeping the original advance, so layout never moves. A 3D rotate turns each unit about its pivot, R = Rz·Ry·Rx.

**Cost:** 10 to 20 ns per glyph per selector per frame; blur adds MTSDF softness or one blur per glyph; glyph_shift's set shapes once at check. Budget class: any class with text.

**It can never:** Run JavaScript; shape per frame; split a grapheme; read the clock; shift a glyph in a number, a counter or a bound value.

**Lands:** R6, with the animator

#### Motion blur

**Fields**

- `scope: declared moves`
- `shutter_angle: deg = 180`; `phase: centred`
- `samples: u8 = 8`; `adaptive: bool = true` (skips under 0.5 px of travel)
- `exclude: [ID]`
- `preview_cap: u8` (labelled when used)

**Semantics:** An exposure window centered on the frame's time after the look's and its placements' quantize, with fixed stratified samples of the pure evaluation, averaged in linear light. Each sample adds its shutter offset after that quantize and is never quantized again, so every frame of a held drawing shows the same blur. A value that holds between its own steps (a quantize key or modifier, a hold array, a physics output with `interpolate: hold`) takes its frame-time value in every sample. Export equals seek. A preview may cap the samples, and says so.

**Cost:** Samples × the moving items' draw cost

**It can never:** Use an accumulation buffer; blur a status color or text during a reading hold; feed a check

**Lands:** R6

#### Motion blur: velocity

For: real-time previews of showpieces (the castle flythrough), physics labs with fast balls, film previews

**Fields**

- `method: samples | velocity = samples` (one method for live and export alike)
- `velocity: {taps: u8 = 16, max: px = 32, tile: px = 20}`

**Semantics:** Velocities come from the pure evaluation at t − s/2 and t + s/2, where s is the shutter and t the frame's time after quantize, with held values at their frame-time value as in Motion blur, so no earlier frame is read. A tile-max and neighbor-max reconstruction filter with fixed taps, offset by a pixel hash, blurs along them. A samples document may preview with velocity under preview_cap, labelled, as samples previews are now.

**Cost:** Two extra transform evaluations of moving items (about 100 ns each), a 4-byte velocity target per pixel, about 0.5 ms at 1080p (estimate). Budget class: showpiece, export previews.

**It can never:** Read the previous frame's transforms or pixels; blur a status color or text during a reading hold; feed a check.

**Lands:** R6

#### Tempo map and cue alignment

**Fields**

- Tempo map: `segments: [{at: "bar:beat" | time (first segment only), bpm, meter, span: beats (rational, so 2.5 is allowed), ramp: none | {to_bpm, shape: linear_in_beats}}]`
- Cue: `{cue: strip | marker, anchor: word | onset | peak | beat | occurrence | moment | marker, offset: flick, move: picture | sound, snap: bool, tolerance: flick, land: frame | sample = frame}` (land applies to move: sound)

**Semantics:** Segments chain: each starts where the previous one ends. Beat to time is closed form, t = t0 + 60·N ÷ (b1 − b0) · ln(bpm(x) ÷ b0) for a ramp linear in beats (60·x ÷ b0 without one), in pinned math rounded to flicks; a segment given an explicit time more than 1 flick from its chained start is refused, naming both. Cues resolve from the tempo map and bakes at check, and a rebake reports moved cues as a diff. Declared onsets (a score's `note_on` lists, strips placed with align) land on their moment's flick within one sample; measured onsets (an onset bake) land within a stated tolerance (±2 ms proposed for percussive presets), and an attack longer than 30 ms cues with `anchor: peak` or a pre-roll. With `land: frame`, the default for move: sound, the onset lands on ⌈moment ÷ Δ⌉ · Δ at the export rate, the first frame that shows the moment. A cue whose moment or anchor doesn't resolve is BLOCKED and named. A literal time in a film with a tempo map raises the notice `literal_time_with_tempo_map`, offering the bar:beat or @marker form. Audio is the master in playback; in export the A/V offset is measured on raw frames and PCM.

**Cost:** O(C log W) per change; nothing per frame

**It can never:** Analyze live where a bake would do; use device clocks in export; move a cue silently; land a sound before the frame that shows its moment

**Lands:** R6

#### Timeline from the record

**Fields**

- `record: {subject: handle, read: [event kind], as_of: ev handle, map: line@1, compress: {merge_within: s = 2, run_merge_within: s = 60, min_dwell: s = 0.36, dwell: {verdict: 1.2, send_back: 0.8, ask: 0.8, merge: 0.6} s, max_gap: s = 1.1, gap_labels: over 2 min}, captions_hold: bool = true, fit_to: duration, lead_in: s, hold_end: s = 1.2, live: bool}`
- The agent writes only event shots, the title and the narration script.
- One station model: lifecycle stations from the ask-task states (task, defining, working, says done, checks, needs you, proven or closed), with one chip per requirement at the checks station

**Semantics:** Builds keys and markers from catalogd events and appends live; `fit_to` rescales gaps, never the order, and every generated marker carries its event IDs. Anchored captions set each beat's minimum dwell, so a script too long for the fit lengthens the film or fails the audit. The record-replay check (section 10) holds it to the projections.

**Cost:** O(events) to build; O(1) per append; 30 lines under 2 ms per frame

**It can never:** Show a state the projections don't; reorder events; color a station except through a status binding

**Lands:** R1

#### Cue list `cues@1`

For: a film or figure an agent writes as plays and waits in order, the way a scene script reads, without computing key times

**Fields**

- `cues: [cue] ≤ 512` (in order)
- Cue: `{id, when: after | with | at: time = after, gap: flick = 0, span: flick = "1s", ease: name = sigmoid(10), lag: ratio | flick = 0, order: index | reverse | seeded = index, targets: [ID | collection], set: {path → value}, kind: cue.kind@1 entry, params}`; a cue with only `span` is a wait
- `cue.kind@1` registry (Registry and seal: registries), which the motion module declares and first-party packs and packs fill: an entry is a pack kind (Pack: kinds in any pack) over the cue signature `{targets, span, ease, lag, order, from: {path → value}, params}`, whose steps write only its targets' channels, placements and markers and the derived items it makes. The first-party verbs ship as a first-party pack, each keeping its name, `since` and digest: enter `create`, `write`, `draw_then_fill`, `fade_in {shift: vec, from: ID | point, scale: f32 = 1}`, `grow {from: point | center | edge: dir | start}`, `spin_in {angle: deg = 90}`, `spiral_in {scale: f32 = 8, fade: 0..1 = 0.3}`, `by_letter`, `by_word`, `type {cursor: ID}`, `in_turn`; exit `uncreate`, `unwrite`, `fade_out {shift, to, scale}`, `shrink`; emphasis `indicate {scale: f32 = 1.2, role = accent}`, `flash {lines: u8 = 12, radius: u}`, `circumscribe {shape: rect | circle = rect, buff: u = 10}`, `passing_flash {width: 0..1 = 0.1}`, `wiggle {scale: f32 = 1.1, angle: deg = 3.6, count: u8 = 6}`, `blink {count: u8 = 1}`, `focus {opacity: f32 = 0.2}`, `broadcast {copies: u8 = 5}`; move `move_along {path: ID}`, `rotate {angle: deg, about: ID#anchor | point}`, `swap {with: ID}`, `cycle`; change `morph {to: ID}`, `match {to: ID, by: id | shape}`, `count_to {value}`, `warp {warp: ID}`

**Semantics:** Expanded at check, never per frame, into channels, placements and markers the cue list owns, with exact flicks. `after` starts a cue at the previous cue's end plus `gap`, `with` at the previous cue's start, and `at` at a time or a marker. Each cue's from-values are what its targets hold at its start, by the same pure evaluation, so a move written after a turn starts where the turn left off. A cue over several targets staggers them by `lag`, for a span of d × ((n − 1) × lag + 1). Each cue also writes a marker `cues.<id>`, so narration, sound and later cues can anchor to it. A verb is a recipe over the existing primitives (path build, trim, repeater, echo, text animator, constraints, pulse), and only the expander is the motion module's code; `circumscribe` reads its target's evaluated bounds over the cue's span. The verbs' math@1 names (Create, FadeIn, Indicate, Circumscribe and the rest) come from math@1's mapping table (Pack: math@1 math-film words). Two cues that write one path at once are refused naming both, unless the second is a `pulse` or an add placement, which add. Every `cue.kind@1` entry passes the cue kit before it's admitted: it expands to identical bytes twice; it writes only paths under its targets and its own derived items; every key it writes lies inside [start, start + d × ((n − 1) × lag + 1)]; an enter verb ends with its targets fully drawn and an exit verb at opacity 0 or unbuilt; and an emphasis verb leaves every path it wrote at its base value, bit for bit, as a pulse does. The kit's planted entries, an `indicate` that ends at scale 1.0000001, a `fade_in` whose last key lands one flick past its span and a verb that writes a non-target's path, must fail, each naming the verb. A pack's verb, `<pack>.<verb>`, is data, so adding one changes no canvas module.

**Cost:** O(cues × targets) at check, under 10 ms for 512 cues (estimate); then as the channels it writes.

**It can never:** Run code; loop or branch; reorder cues silently; read the clock; write a path another item's channel owns.

**Lands:** R6

Also decided: springs had three conventions (Hz and ζ in physics, stiffness 64 and damping 16 in the figure kit, none on channels); all use Hz and a damping ratio, and the kit's spring is 1.27 Hz at ζ 1. The keyed follow and the films dry run's follow models are one `follow`. Time fields are `t`, never `at`. The marker kind `scene` is `shot`, and `event` splits into `moment` (a checked instant) and `record` (from record events). The R1 line needs markers and placement start, span, series and stagger, so those land in R1, earlier than the tech design's R6 for the whole row; `child_of` lands with parenting in R1 for the same reason. One station model resolves the line's per-requirement stations against the claim film's lifecycle stations.

### The closed function list

Drivers and fields share these functions and nothing else. Each is pure Rust in f64 with pinned math (the `libm` crate, through one ops module, which the core owns with the `ease@1` registry, so a build without motion still evaluates `ease(name, x)`), so results match across machines; a lint refuses std transcendental methods, clocks, thread RNG and glam's SIMD types in every crate whose output a check reads. Each function also has an interval form in the same pinned math, widened by its implementation's error bound, which returns a range certain to hold the function's value over a range of its inputs, and so do the eases, the key interpolations and the samplers that read clips and bakes. The certainty is interval arithmetic's: each form bounds its function by its monotone pieces and known extrema, such as sin's peaks at π/2 + 2kπ, widens that by the error bound and rounds its lower end down and its upper end up, so it holds every value the function takes over the range, and an expression evaluated through the forms holds every value the expression takes. Seeded and property tests only search for counterexamples; they never prove that a form holds. A check that needs a bound over x, a span of time, a step or a control's range takes it from these forms, never from samples alone (Path `path@1`: function, Camera `camera@1`: framing, Check input: loop kinds: camera paths, Constraint: spring chain, Control sweep), and a value the forms can't settle within the check's budget is an estimate, which never decides a check: a check that needs the bound there is refused, naming the item and the range, never passed on its samples.

| Group | Functions |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic and logic | `+ - * / % ^`, `== != < <= > >= && \|\| !`, `c ? a : b`, `min max clamp abs sign floor ceil fract round mod` |
| Powers and angles | `sqrt pow exp log sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 deg rad`; constants `pi tau` |
| Hyperbolic and special | `sinh cosh tanh asinh acosh atanh`, `log2 log10 log1p expm1 hypot cbrt`, `sinc(x)` (sin x ÷ x, 1 at 0), `erf erfc`, `gamma lgamma`, `factorial(n)` (n an integer, 0 to 170), `binom(n, k)` |
| Interpolation | `mix smoothstep remap(x, a, b, c, d) ease(name, x)`, with names from the `ease@1` registry (Channel and key: table eases) |
| Vectors | `vec2 vec3 vec4`, swizzles, `length distance dot cross normalize angle(a, b)` |
| Complex, as vec2 | `cmul cdiv cexp clog cpow csqrt csin ccos conj cabs carg`, over vec2 read as x + yi; `clog` and `carg` take the principal branch |
| Bounded sums | `sum(k, a, b, term)`, `prod(k, a, b, term)`: k runs over the integers a to b; each bound is a literal or a var with a declared max; at most 256 terms |
| Seeded | `hash(…) → [0, 1)`, a fixed 32-bit integer hash; `noise(p, seed)`, gradient noise on the integer lattice hash; `rand(key[, lo, hi])` = hash(the item's seed, key) mapped to [lo, hi), never a stream, so adding one call never shifts another |
| Occurrence lists | `since(list) last(list) next(list) rank(list) count(list, a, b) inside(list)`. Over a list a var binds with an optional filter (kinds, `a`, `b`, tags and `where`, as Spawn's `on` takes), each reads the matches at or before t and takes the driver's fallback when none matches: `count(list)` the matches so far, and `count(list, a, b)` those between the stable IDs a and b, in either order; `last(list)` the latest match's flick, and `since(list)` t minus it; `next(list)` the next match's flick, refused as a look-ahead is when inputs feed the list; `rank(list)` the latest match's index, from 0; `inside(list)` 1 while t lies inside a match's span, else 0. A payload field reads as `last(list).field` or `next(list).field`, such as `last(landings).point.x`, `speed` or `impulse` |
| Input track | `since_change(control) held(control) follow(control, span, ease)` |
| View | `hovered(id)`; `hover_at(id) → vec2`, the pointer's position over the item's bounds from 0 to 1 on each axis, or (−1, −1) off it, as Overlay: clamped to the edge says (viewer class; never saved) |
| Time offsets (drivers only) | `lag(var, dt)`, the var's value at t − dt, with dt a literal within ±10 s; `smooth(var, width, samples)`, the mean of lag over a window centered on t, at most 16 samples (Driver: time offsets) |
| Tables | `table(name, x)`: a function table's value at x, linear or monotone between its knots and held at its ends, with an interval form exact from its knots (Driver: tables) |

`rand` exists only as a keyed hash. `step` is left out, since step means a physics step; `x >= edge ? 1 : 0` does the same.

A removable singularity is a function of its own: sinc's interval form holds 1 at 0, so sin(x)/x written as sinc(x) plots through 0 without a break. A sum's interval form is the sum of its terms' forms, and a term past a var bound's value adds exactly 0, so a slider that changes N never breaks a curve. A sum counts its term's nodes times its count against the expression's cap: 64 ops for a driver, 256 nodes for a field, 512 for a path function. Complex forms bound boxes, not discs. A sum can never loop past 256 terms, take a bound with no declared max or recurse, and factorial never takes a non-integer.

<a id="physics"></a>

## A timeline as data over a pinned backend

- **The timeline.** The physics module keeps a timeline, as data, over Rapier pinned to an exact version: every input recorded, a cheap state hash each step, replay that names the first diverging step and field, a checkpoint ring with a byte budget, and baked playback that never re-simulates.
- **Declared choices.** Documents declare combine rules and defaults, because engines disagree on them, and swapping backends must not change results silently.
- **Conventions.** State is f32. IDs are stable document IDs, never engine handles, and order is canonical by (priority, ID).

#### World and backend `physics.world@1`

**Fields**

- `dimensions: 2 | 3 = 3`
- `step_rate: Hz = 120` (under the valid-rates rule)
- `substeps: 1 to 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 15 | 16 = 4`
- `span: flick = 60 s` (at most 10 min; on disk past 1 min)
- `gravity: vec, m/s² = (0, −9.81, 0)`
- `seed: u64 = the document's seed`
- `mode: dynamic | kinematic = dynamic`
- `capacity: {bodies, shapes, joints, contacts, particles: u32}` (required)
- `solver: {contact_hz: Hz = 30, contact_damping = 10, max_speed: m/s = 400, restitution_threshold: m/s = 0, hit_threshold: m/s = 1, sleep: {on: bool = true, speed: m/s = 0.05, time: s = 0.5}, ccd: bool = true}`
- `combine: {friction: geometric | average | min | max | multiply = geometric, restitution: the same set = max}`
- `defaults: {friction = 0.5, restitution = 0, damping = 0}`
- `contact_materials: {ID → contact material}`
- `checkpoint: {every: steps = 60, budget: bytes = 16 MiB}`
- `budget: {step_p95: ms = 2, memory: MB = 50, bake_10s: ms = 1,000}`
- `backend: {name: rapier2d | rapier3d, version: =0.36.1, features: [enhanced-determinism, serde-serialize], excluded: [simd8, parallel], threads: 1, libm: pure Rust, target, target_features: baseline, rustc}`
- Backend interface: `id() caps() build(doc) step(inputs) occurrences() read(state) query(ray | sweep | overlap) move_character(body, translation) drive_vehicle(body) hash() checkpoint() restore()`

**Semantics:** Building a world creates everything in canonical order or returns issues. A world runs inside each scene that lists it: its outputs' item paths and its bodies' follow channels resolve in that scene, its inputs are entries on that scene's one input track, and its occurrence list is named `<world ID>.occurrences` there. Each step: apply the inputs stamped for it, ordered by kind then target ID; set kinematic targets from channels at t(k+1); move each character body through the backend's character controller, which sets its kinematic target (Body `body@1`: character); update each vehicle body through the backend's vehicle controller, whose wheels push its chassis (Body `body@1`: vehicle); add forces from the state at t(k); run the backend step, whose substeps are the solver's iterations, not repeated steps; read and sort occurrences; write state into a two-step ring; take the cheap hash. `caps()` decides what the document check refuses. `query()` answers a ray, a sweep or an overlap against the state the last step left, collision groups applied, and `physics.query`, `physics.cast@1` and `nav.reach` reach the backend only through it; `move_character()` is the character controller a character body moves through (Body `body@1`: character), and `drive_vehicle()` the vehicle controller a vehicle body drives through (Body `body@1`: vehicle). The behavior kit tests all three. The interface absorbs 0.36's API break: its step takes the soft-body set with the rigid ones, and a snapshot from before 0.36 doesn't load, so no checkpoint or bake crosses that version and no world document sees it. Rapier 0.36.1 has no `simd` or `fast-math` feature: its four-wide SIMD solver always runs and is part of its cross-platform promise, `simd8` breaks that promise, and enhanced determinism forces scalar math through libm. The crate builds for the target's baseline features, never `target-cpu=native` or `+fma`, as Rapier's own cross-architecture goldens do. Rapier caps each body's speed at `max_speed` and its turn at 45° a step, and a body it caps writes `fault {kind: speed_cap}` naming it, so no cap is silent. It has no restitution threshold: a new contact with restitution bounces at any approach speed, and one that persists into the next step rests, so `caps()` refuses a `restitution_threshold` other than 0. While sound plays, a live world steps until its time is at least one audio block past the timeline position of the first sample not yet written, before that block renders, so it holds while the timeline holds (Marker: present mode), so a spawn starts each of its occurrences on its own sample; a step that isn't ready in time counts an underrun in the device gate's stats and never moves a voice. The exception is restitution 1 or more: such a contact never rests, so a cradle of touching balls passes momentum along. Rapier is the reference implementation of the physics interface, `physics@1`, declared `measured` with `backend_bytes` state (Canvas module: interface and implementation), and any backend, Rapier included, passes the world's behavior fixtures within their tolerances before a build can choose it (Physics: behavior kit).

**Cost:** Per step ≈ a × awake bodies + b × contacts × substeps + c × joints × substeps + d × bodies × forces; 2D joints about 56 ns per joint-substep (estimate); a deep checkpoint about 4 KB per body

**It can never:** Run code per step; read the wall clock; run on the GPU when it feeds a check; grow past its capacity; build with fast math or features that change results

**Lands:** R6

#### Shape

**Fields**

- `kind: sphere {radius: m} | box {half: vec3, m} | capsule {half_height, radius: m} | cylinder {half_height, radius: m} | convex {points ≤ 64 (≤ 8 in 2D), radius: m = 0} | plane {normal} | mesh {vertices, triangles} | heightfield {cols, rows, heights, scale} | compound {children: [{shape, pose}]}`
- 2D: `circle | segment {a, b} | polygon (≤ 8) | chain {points, loop: bool}`
- Each use on a body: `{shape, offset: pose, contact_material, collision_group, sensor: bool = false, sensor_test: center | overlap = overlap}`

**Semantics:** Built once at load and shared by ID. Convex hulls and decompositions are computed at load and cached under the bake key. Mesh, heightfield, plane and chain shapes are static only.

**Cost:** Narrow phase per pair: sphere and capsule are cheapest, then box, then convex(n), then mesh; a mesh takes about 24 B per triangle plus its BVH

**It can never:** Be a dynamic mesh, heightfield, plane or chain; change shape mid-run

**Lands:** R6

#### Body `body@1`

**Fields**

- `kind: static | kinematic | dynamic | character | vehicle` (character: Body `body@1`: character; vehicle: Body `body@1`: vehicle)
- `shapes: [shape use]`
- `pose: {pos: m, rot: quat | deg}`
- `velocity: {linear: m/s = 0, angular: deg/s = 0}`
- `mass: kg` (else density × volume); `inertia` (optional)
- `damping: {linear: 1/s = 0, angular: 1/s = 0}`
- `gravity_scale: f32 = 1`; `ccd: bool = false`; `sleep: bool = true`
- `locks: {linear, angular: [bool; 3]}`
- `follow: channel path` (kinematic only)
- `active: bool = true`
- `anchors: {name → local point, m}`
- `priority: i32 = 0`

**Semantics:** A dynamic body is integrated by the backend. A kinematic body moves to its `follow` target at t(k+1) over the step; that channel is evaluated at t(k+1) inside the step, before the solve. An inactive body is skipped until an `activate` input; a body that appears mid-run is declared inactive and activated.

**Cost:** O(1) per awake body per substep; about 0 while asleep

**It can never:** Be created mid-run; be moved except by its channel or a recorded input

**Lands:** R6

#### Body `body@1`: character

For: bounded games and labs with someone who walks: a platformer's hero, a guard on patrol, a visitor who tours a house

**Fields**

- `kind: character` (on `body@1`, whose `shapes` then hold one capsule, with no `follow`)
- `character: {slope_limit: deg = 45, step: {height: m = 0.3, width: m = the capsule's radius}, snap: m = 0.2, offset: m = 0.01, jump: {height: m = 1}}`
- Inputs: `move {velocity: vec, m/s}` (the walk it wants, held until its next move); `jump {height: m}` (optional; else its own)
- Outputs: `read: grounded | sliding | velocity | pose`
- State: `{wants: vec, vertical: m/s, grounded: bool, sliding: bool, touching: [shape use]}` (in every checkpoint and hash; touching: the shapes its controller touched in its last step, which its next step's `contact_begin` and `contact_end` compare against; grounded: a walkable surface lies within `offset` + 0.05 m below the capsule; sliding: it stands on a surface steeper than `slope_limit` and moves down it)

**Semantics:** A kinematic capsule that the backend's character controller moves, behind the backend interface, so no backend type reaches a document. The behavior below is the physics interface's, not a backend's: every backend's controller, Rapier's first, must show it in the behavior kit's character fixtures before a build can choose that backend (Physics: behavior kit). Its up is against the world's gravity, or +Y in a world with none. Each step, after the step's inputs apply and before forces and the backend step, each character body moves in canonical (priority, ID) order against the world as the last step left it. With g the size of the world's gravity, off the ground its vertical speed first falls by g × gravity_scale × the step's length; on the ground it's 0, and a jump on a grounded step sets it to √(2 × g × gravity_scale × height) instead, while a jump off the ground does nothing. The controller then moves the capsule by (wants + up × vertical) × the step's length, sliding along what it meets and keeping `offset` from it: a slope steeper than `slope_limit` stops its climb and slides it down, a step no higher than `step.height` with `step.width` free on top lifts it, and moving down from the ground it snaps to ground within `snap`. Its new pose is its kinematic target for the backend step. Dynamic bodies stop it as static shapes do, and it pushes none. Each shape its controller touches in a step that it didn't touch the step before writes `contact_begin` naming it, and each it leaves writes `contact_end`, sorted with the rest. Outputs read `grounded`, `sliding`, its pose and `velocity`, the move it made over the step's length, so logic reads them as earlier steps left them and items draw from them. Its state joins every checkpoint beside the backend's, and the cheap and canonical hashes after the bodies', so a seek restores it and steps forward, and seeking equals playing. A rig or a skinned asset draws on it through its pose; the body only moves. `caps()` says whether the backend has a character controller, and a world with a character body on one that doesn't is refused, naming the body and the backend.

**Cost:** A few shape casts a step per character body: about 20 to 60 µs at 120 Hz in a level of a few hundred static shapes (estimate); its state about 32 B in each checkpoint. Budget class: as the world.

**It can never:** Move except by its inputs, its controller and gravity; climb a slope steeper than its limit or a step higher than its step height; pass into a static shape; push a dynamic body; hold a shape other than one capsule

**Lands:** R6, after the physics module

#### Body `body@1`: vehicle

For: small driving games and labs: a kart on a track, a rover on a dune, a product car you can drive around a showroom

**Fields**

- `kind: vehicle` (on `body@1`: a dynamic chassis whose `shapes` are its body, with no `follow`; 3D worlds only)
- `vehicle: {wheels: {name → {at: local point, m, radius: m, suspension: {rest: m, travel: m, hz: f32, damping_ratio: f32 = 0.3}, grip: f32 = 1, steers: bool = false, drives: bool = false, brakes: bool = true}} ≤ 8, steer_max: deg = 35}` (each wheel's ray points down the chassis's −Y, its axle along X and its heading along +Z)
- Inputs: `drive {force: N}` (the push the driving wheels share equally, negative to reverse); `steer {angle: deg}` (a positive angle turns the heading about +Y, to the left); `brake {force: N}` (the braking force the braking wheels share equally); each held until its next
- Outputs: the body's own reads, and on a wheel's address `<body>#<wheel>`, `pose` (its hub at its suspension's length, turned by its steer and its spin) and `contact_count` (0 or 1)
- State: `{wheels: [{spin: deg, spin_rate: deg, touching: bool}], drive: N, steer: deg, brake: N}` (in every checkpoint and hash; spin_rate: the turn the wheel made in its last step, which it keeps, decaying, while off the ground)

**Semantics:** A dynamic chassis on ray-cast wheels that the backend's vehicle controller drives, behind the backend interface, so no backend type reaches a document; the character body's sibling. The behavior below is the physics interface's, not a backend's: every backend's controller, Rapier's first, must show it in the behavior kit's vehicle fixtures before a build can choose that backend (Physics: behavior kit). Each step, after character bodies move and before forces and the backend step, each vehicle body in canonical (priority, ID) order casts each wheel's ray from `at` down its chassis, over `rest` + `radius`, against the world as the last step left it; a wheel whose ray meets a shape touches it, its suspension's length the hit's distance less its radius, kept within `rest` ± `travel`. A touching wheel's spring pushes the chassis along the ray by k × (`rest` − length), with k = (m ÷ n) × (2π × `hz`)² for a chassis of mass m on n wheels, so the chassis bounces at `hz` and settles g ÷ (2π × `hz`)² on level ground, and its damping follows `damping_ratio` on the same share of the mass. `drive` pushes each touching driving wheel along its heading; `brake` resists each touching braking wheel's rolling, up to its share, and never pushes it backwards, and while `brake` is above 0 no wheel drives; a `drive` other than 0 wakes the body; and each touching wheel's grip resists its sideways slip, up to `grip` × the load its spring carries. `steer` turns the steering wheels by Ackermann's rule: with δ the steer angle, clamped so the wheel inside the turn stays within `steer_max`, L the distance from the steering wheels' axle to the other wheels' axle, or to the middle of the other axles where there are several, and w the track between a steering pair, the wheel inside the turn takes atan(L ÷ (L ÷ tan δ − w ÷ 2)) and the one outside atan(L ÷ (L ÷ tan δ + w ÷ 2)), so at low speed the middle of the other axle circles at L ÷ tan δ. A touching wheel's spin turns by its contact's forward travel ÷ its radius, and a wheel off the ground keeps turning by its last step's turn, which falls by 1% a step; spin only draws the wheel, and no check reads it. Each wheel whose ray starts or stops meeting a shape writes `contact_begin` or `contact_end` naming the body and the wheel, sorted with the rest. Its state joins every checkpoint beside the backend's, and the cheap and canonical hashes after the bodies', so a seek restores it and steps forward, and seeking equals playing. Built items, a rig or a skinned asset draw on it through its pose and its wheels' poses; the body only moves. `caps()` says whether the backend has a vehicle controller, and a world with a vehicle body on one that doesn't, or in a 2D world, is refused, naming the body and the backend.

**Cost:** One ray a wheel a step, plus the controller's pushes: about 5 to 15 µs at 120 Hz for a four-wheeled body (estimate); its state about 64 B in each checkpoint. Budget class: as the world.

**It can never:** Move except by its wheels, its inputs, its contacts, gravity and the forces and joints its world declares on it; steer past `steer_max`; brake a wheel backwards; hold more than 8 wheels; run in a 2D world

**Lands:** R6, after the physics module, beside the character body

#### Breakable `breakable@1`

For: physics labs (a tower of blocks that shatters, a beam that snaps at its weakest bond), films (a wall that crumbles under a wrecking ball)

**Fields**

- `pieces: asset ID` (a fracture asset: pieces, hulls, bonds and the source mesh, from Asset job kind fracture)
- `at: transform`; `contact_material`; `collision_group`
- `strength: {per_level: [N] | from: contact_material}` (bond strength)
- `anchored: {region: box | plane, m} | [piece]` (optional; pieces held static)
- `release: {inherit: velocity, spin: bool = true}`
- `max_active: u16 = 512` (the pool of piece bodies declared at build)

**Semantics:** A breakable starts as one compound body; after each step, under the default contact loading, the wrapper adds each contact's impulse to the bonds it loads, in canonical order, and a bond past its strength breaks and writes a break occurrence. Stress loading spreads gravity and impulses through the whole bond graph instead (Breakable: stress loading). Pieces cut off from the rest become bodies from the pool declared at build, moving with the parent's velocity at their centroids, so no body appears mid-run. Checkpoints hold the active set, and under stress loading the bond forces kept as its warm start, so a seek restores the nearest one and steps forward. While no bond has broken, the breakable draws the fracture asset's source mesh in one draw; from the step of its first break it draws its pieces. The choice reads only the active set, so cut seams never show on an intact wall and seeking still equals playing.

**Cost:** Per step O(bonds that contacts load) plus released pieces as bodies; a 300-piece wall is about 0.5 to 2 ms per 120 Hz step while breaking (estimate); checkpoints grow about 4 KB per active piece. Budget class: work product (labs), export (films).

**It can never:** Create a body mid-run; break through a callback; draw randomness that isn't keyed to IDs.

**Lands:** R6, after the physics module

#### Breakable: stress loading

For: physics labs (a beam that snaps at its weakest bond, a tower that gives way where it's weakest), films (a wall whose base is shot out falls apart before it lands)

**Fields**

- `load: contact | stress = contact` (on `breakable@1`)
- `stress: {iterations: u8 = 12 (≤ 64), gravity: bool = true}`

**Semantics:** Under stress loading, gravity and contact impulses spread through the bond graph every awake step. Nodes are the pieces in canonical order, with mass from density × volume; anchored pieces are fixed nodes, and each contact impulse enters at the nearest piece's centroid. The solve runs exactly `iterations` per step, warm-started from the previous step's bond forces, which the checkpoint holds, and never tests for convergence, so a step stays bounded and the same on every machine. A bond breaks when its tension, compression or shear passes that mode's strength (Contact material: strength; a per-level strength in N applies to all three) and writes the existing break occurrence; released pieces split off by union-find in bond order. A sleeping breakable runs no pass. The math is scalar, through the one ops module, with no callbacks.

**Cost:** O(iterations × bonds) per awake step: about 900 bonds at 12 iterations is 0.2 to 1 ms per 120 Hz step on one core (estimate); checkpoints grow about 12 B per bond. Budget class: as the world.

**It can never:** Iterate to convergence or change its iteration count during a run; keep a bond's health or damage between steps; run through a callback or on the GPU; run while the breakable sleeps.

**Lands:** R6, with `breakable@1`

#### Contact material

**Fields**

- `friction: f32 = 0.5`
- `restitution: f32 = 0`
- `density: kg/m³` (kg/m² in 2D; required unless the body sets its mass)
- `rolling_resistance: f32 = 0`
- `tangent_speed: m/s = 0`
- `tag: string` (such as "wood")

**Semantics:** The two sides of a contact combine by the world's combine rule. Sounds map from tags in the media module's spawn rules, never from the material. Rapier has no rolling resistance or tangent speed, so on it `caps()` refuses `rolling_resistance` and `tangent_speed` other than 0, naming the field; a ball that should roll to rest takes angular damping (Body).

**Cost:** O(1) per contact

**It can never:** Carry a sound or code; combine through a callback

**Lands:** R6

#### Contact material: strength

For: breakable bonds that take their strength from the material (stone breaks before steel)

**Fields**

- `strength: N/m² | {tension, compression, shear: N/m²}` (optional; the stress at which a bond breaks; one number sets all three modes)

**Semantics:** Under contact loading, a bond between two pieces breaks when the contact impulses that load it in one step, divided by the step time and its contact area, pass the smallest strength on either side; no load carries to the next step. Under stress loading (Breakable: stress loading), it breaks when its tension, compression or shear stress passes that mode's strength, the lower of its two sides'.

**Cost:** None beyond `breakable@1`'s per-step bond update. Budget class: as the world.

**It can never:** Carry code; depend on the run.

**Lands:** R6

#### Collision group

**Fields**

- World: `collision_groups: [name]` (at most 32)
- Each shape use: `member: [name]`, `collides: [name]`
- Each joint: `collide_connected: bool = false`

**Semantics:** Two shapes interact when each one's `member` meets the other's `collides`. A sensor reports overlaps and never responds.

**Cost:** One bit test per broad-phase pair

**It can never:** Be decided by code (no filter callbacks); exceed 32 groups

**Lands:** R6

#### Joint `joint@1`

**Fields**

- `kind: fixed | ball | hinge | slider | distance | rope | gear | rack | pulley | path`
- `a, b: body ID[#anchor] | soft ID#cluster | world`
- `frame_a, frame_b: {anchor: m, axis}`
- `limits: {min, max}` (deg or m; a hinge's range under 360°)
- `spring: {hz, damping_ratio = 1, rest}`
- `motor: {mode: velocity | position, target: number | channel path, max_force: N | max_torque: N·m, hz, damping_ratio}`
- `breaks_at: {force: N, torque: N·m, over_steps: u8 = 1}`
- `ratio: f32` (gear, rack, pulley); `of: [joint ID]` (gear: two hinges; rack: a hinge and a slider)
- `pulley: {ground_a, ground_b: m, length_min, length_max: m}`
- `path: {curve: ID, rotation: free | tangent | fixed}`
- `active: bool = true`

**Semantics:** Motor targets read their channels at t(k+1). After each step, force = the impulse of the joint's locks and limits ÷ the length of the substep it came from, never its motor's, which only `max_force` or `max_torque` bounds; `joint_force` reads the same force, and past `breaks_at` for `over_steps` steps the joint is disabled at the start of the next step and a `break` occurrence is written. A hinge's `joint_coordinate` counts whole turns: it is the angle between its bodies, which wraps at ±180°, plus 360° for each turn, counted when a step's shortest signed change crosses the wrap, and the turn count and the steps it has spent past `breaks_at` are the joint's state, kept in checkpoints and the state hash. A step whose relative angular speed would turn a hinge 180° or more writes `fault {kind: speed_cap}`, since its turn can't be told from a wrap.
